newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-TEENAGE KEEPER NOTCHES UP REMARKABLE RECORD.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-TEENAGE KEEPER NOTCHES UP REMARKABLE RECORD.

text.p: He is not yet 18 and has not yet been on the losing side in 24 consecutive French first division matches for Nantes since his first match last October.
Meet goalkeeper Mickael Landreau, whose maturity both on and off the field has surprised everyone, except perhaps his mother Odile.

Far from being intimidated when Lubomir Moravcik's studs grazed his cheek on a tough debut in the cauldron of Bastia's Furiani stadium on Corsica, Landreau later saved the Slovakian midfielder's penalty to keep the score at 0-0.
Landreau, who won his place because of injury to Dominique Casagrande and reserve Eric Loussouarn's poor form, was 17 years and four months old.
Four days later, Nantes had so recovered their confidence after failing to notch up a victory in their first 10 games of the season that they crushed Nice 7-0.

Nantes and Landreau were on their way, the team to an unbeaten run that now stands at 26 matches, the young 'keeper to a run of 24 in which he has conceded only 11 goals, plus the leap from France's junior national team to reserve in the under-21s.

Such was Landreau's importance to Nantes after his first two games that the club chartered a private plane to fetch him from under-18 national team duty in Sweden for their league match at Lille, flying him in the night before.
"What's happening to Micka is not down to us, he's done it all himself," Odile Landreau said in a recent interview in France Football magazine.

"I'm not surprised that he's at ease among players much older than him... He's always lived among adults, if only at home," she said. Landreau has an older brother of 29 and two sisters also in their late 20s.
Landreau, who was a special guest on a French television chat show last Sunday, said: "This (success and fame) hasn't changed anything."
Self-assured beyond his years, Landreau joked with his interviewers and discussed his strengths and weaknesses.
"I don't like aerial shots too much," he said.
Landreau models himself on Fabien Barthez, the Monaco and France goakeeper who won the European Cup with Marseille in 1993 and is aware he still has much to learn from his idol.
With Monaco on the verge of winning the league championship, Barthez and Landreau could both be taking part in the European Cup next season.
The television programme dwelt on Landreau's weakness in the air, showing footage of a rare mistake when he conceded a late equaliser at Marseille in a league match three weeks ago.

It was only the third goal the teenager has conceded in in his last 13 league games as Nantes climbed to third place, one point behind Paris St Germain and in a strong position to fight for France's second European Cup berth.
Jean-Louis Garcia, who trains Nantes's goalkeepers, said Landreau's biggest asset was perhaps his mental strength.
"I remember, at Bastia, the stadium loudspeakers were blaring at their loudest and he was having a laugh. I think it's there, in his mastery over the occasion, that he stands out."
